report.verdict: The US regulated market is still the world's largest and most profitable online pool, but Q3-26 marks the first quarter where the growth engine visibly stalled: iGaming decelerated to +12% YoY (Citizens; +12.3% in August per AGA), sports-betting GGR fell 15.6% YoY in August on a 9.2% hold and flat handle, and the AGA now attributes a structural handle leak to CFTC-regulated "prediction markets" that pay no state gaming tax (est. $1.56bn foregone since Jan-25). For an operator weighing entry, the opportunity has shifted from land-grab to share-take in a seven-state iGaming oligopoly (top-3 = 65.9% share and falling) and to the unresolved federal/state fight over event contracts, which is now the single biggest swing factor for the rulebook.

summary: **Market scale.** AGA State of the States 2026 puts FY2025 US commercial gaming GGR at a record $78.62bn (+9.1% YoY) across 38 jurisdictions, of which sports betting was $16.89bn (+22.6%), iGaming $10.73bn (+27.6%) and traditional slots/tables ~$51.0bn (residual, derived). Direct gaming tax paid to states/localities was $17.86bn (+12.3%). 34–35 jurisdictions set annual records.

**Growth has stalled in Q3-26.** AGA monthly trackers show July GGR ~$6.76bn (+8.6%, World Cup-boosted) but August $6.48bn (-0.6%), the first YoY decline in the series this year. Jul+Aug combined is $13.24bn, +3.9% (computed) versus +9.1% for FY25. The AGA's Q3 quarterly report (incl. September) was not yet published as of 10 Nov 2026.

**Sports betting is the problem child.** August SB GGR fell 15.6% to $1.00bn on handle of $10.89bn (-0.7%); hold compressed to 9.2% from 10.8%. The AGA states that outside June–July (World Cup) national handle has been down YoY every month since December 2025, blaming prediction-market leakage and a later college-football start.
**World Cup was a one-off.** July SB GGR rose 27.0% to $1.27bn on handle +31.9% to $11.60bn (hold ~10.9%, computed, below July-25's ~11.4%). This flattered Q3 and will not recur until 2030.

**iGaming is decelerating but still compounding.** Citizens' Q3-26 read is +12% YoY (vs +16% in Q1/Q2), the slowest on record; AGA monthly prints were +15.7% (Jul, $1.01bn) and +12.3% (Aug, $1.03bn). No new state has launched since Rhode Island (2024); Maine's tribal-iGaming law became effective early 2026 but had not launched at the time of writing.

**Online penetration.** SB (all channels) plus iGaming equalled 35.1% of FY25 commercial GGR, 33.7% in July-26 and 31.3% in August-26 (AGA does not split retail vs online SB in the monthly headline; retail SB is typically a mid-single-digit share of SB GGR).

**iGaming oligopoly loosening.** Citizens Q3-26 share: FanDuel 25.1% (26.6% a year ago, declining every quarter of 2026), DraftKings 22.2% (24.3%; but up from 20.9% in Q2 – first sequential gain in two years), BetMGM 18.6% (20.7%, sixth straight decline), Rush Street 7.4% (6.8%), Caesars 6.4% (7.1%), Fanatics 5.2% (3.9%), bet365 1.7% (0.4%) after MI and WV launches. Top-3 share fell to 65.9% from 71.6%.

**Sportsbook duopoly intact, margins diverging.** Q3-26 GGR share: DraftKings 35.4% (34.9%), FanDuel 35.4% (37.7%) – a combined 70.8%. Handle share DraftKings 37.6%, FanDuel 32.8%, Fanatics 9.9%. Gross gaming margin: FanDuel 10.4%, BetMGM 10.2%, DraftKings 9.5%, bet365 9.4%, Caesars 6.9%; market-wide 9.6%, flat YoY (Citizens).

**State prints confirm the split.** NJ DGE September: iGaming win $274.8m (+13.0%), YTD $2.40bn (+13.2%); sports-wagering GGR $77.0m (-14.3%), YTD $748.4m (-6.3%); total gaming revenue $579.6m (+2.8%). Michigan MGCB September: iGaming gross receipts $300.2m, OSB gross $55.5m on handle $544.8m (+64.9% MoM), 15 licensed operators.

**Licensing is state-by-state and expensive at the top.** Commercial sports betting is live in 35 commercial states (39 states + DC + PR including tribal-only per AGA/CardPlayer); iGaming in 7 (NJ, PA, MI, WV, CT, DE, RI; Nevada poker-only; Maine pending). Access is typically via a land-based/tribal skin partner; headline licence fees range from ~$100k (NJ) to $25m (NY) [statutory figures from prior research, not re-verified this cycle].

**Tax is on GGR, with a 2025 ratchet.** Headline rates run from 6.75% (NV) to 51% (NY, RI). 2025 hikes included NJ to 19.75% (OSB & iGaming), Maryland to 20%, Louisiana to 21.5% and Illinois' tiered 20–40% plus a $0.25/$0.50 per-wager surcharge; federal excise is 0.25% of handle and the OBBBA caps the player loss deduction at 90% from TY2026 [background; unverified this cycle]. No major rate change was identified in Q3-26 itself.

**Tax take is now shrinking in SB.** August gaming tax was $1.46bn (-1.5%); sports-betting tax fell 14.0%. The AGA estimates prediction-market sports contracts have cost states $1.56bn in foregone gaming tax since January 2025 (up from $1.5bn in the July tracker) – the political fuel for state enforcement.

**Enforcement direction is hardening against unlicensed channels.** AGA reports 16 states took enforcement action against sports-event-contract platforms by May 2026; on 28 Oct 2026 the Michigan Gaming Control Board announced Polymarket US (QCX LLC) agreed to stop offering new sports-related contracts in the state. Sweepstakes casinos and skill machines are the other two untaxed targets named by the AGA.

**Product rules are still widening for licensees.** MGCB added fixed-odds horse-race wagering to Michigan online sportsbooks (30 Oct 2026); Resorts World NYC's table-game expansion lifted August national table revenue (+2.1%).

**Payments are card/ACH-based, not mobile-money.** Deposits run through debit, ACH/e-check, PayPal/Venmo, Apple Pay and prepaid Play+; several states bar credit-card deposits (e.g. MA, IA, TN) and the AGA Responsible Marketing Code governs advertising [background; not re-verified]. Compliance cost per state (geofencing, KYC, RG tooling) is material.

**Land-based is low-growth ballast.** Traditional slots/tables were $4.48bn in July (+3.1%) and $4.44bn in August (+0.9%); slots +0.9–1.0%, tables +2.1–6.2%. NJ Atlantic City casino win fell 1.3% in September; Detroit's three casinos earned $103.55m.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** The US is a share-take, not a land-grab, market: iGaming CAC is rising as growth slows, SB economics depend on a tax base that states keep raising and on a hold that is normalising, while an untaxed federal-licensed competitor (event contracts) is pulling handle. Entry economics only clear in the 7 iGaming states or via B2B supply to incumbents; a direct B2C sportsbook launch into the top-5 oligopoly is value-destructive at current CPA levels.

**Catalysts next 6 months.** AGA Q3-26 quarterly report (mid-Nov); September/October state prints (NY Sept hold reported at 6.6% – secondary); federal appellate rulings and any CFTC rulemaking on sports event contracts; Maine iGaming launch; 2027 state sessions (iGaming bills, tax hikes); the 90% loss-deduction cap biting in the 2026 tax year.

segments.name: Sports betting (retail + online)
segments.headline: World Cup masked a structural handle stall; August GGR -15.6% on 9.2% hold, with prediction markets now an acknowledged leak.
narrative: The AGA's two Q3 monthly trackers tell opposite stories that net to a weak quarter. July sports-betting GGR rose 27.0% YoY to $1.27bn on handle of $11.60bn (+31.9%), the first material handle growth since December 2025, entirely attributable to the FIFA World Cup; the computed hold of ~10.9% was below July 2025's ~11.4%, so revenue growth lagged volume. August then reversed: handle slipped 0.7% to $10.89bn, hold fell to 9.2% from 10.8%, and GGR dropped 15.6% to $1.00bn. The AGA explicitly states that outside June and July, national handle has declined year-on-year in every month since December 2025, and attributes August's weakness to sports contracts on so-called prediction markets and a later college-football start. Combined Jul+Aug GGR of $2.27bn is +3.9% YoY (computed) on handle +13.8%, i.e. the quarter's growth is a World Cup artefact.

State September prints point to a soft close to the quarter. New Jersey's sports-wagering gross revenue fell 14.3% YoY to $77.0m and is down 6.3% YTD at $748.4m, even as total state gaming revenue rose 2.8% – a clean read that the leak is specific to sportsbook, not to gambling demand. Michigan's online handle rebounded 64.9% MoM to $544.8m with the NFL (gross receipts $55.5m, implying ~10.2% gross hold; adjusted gross receipts after promo deductions only $24.89m, underlining how heavy promotional write-offs remain in a mature state). New York's September mobile handle was reported at ~$2.4bn with a 6.6% hold (secondary headline, unverified), which if confirmed implies a sharp YoY GGR decline in the largest state. The AGA's pre-season forecast of $29.5bn in legal NFL betting was framed as growth stalling.

Citizens' Q3-26 share data (secondary; based on reporting states) show the duopoly entrenched at a combined 70.8% of GGR, but with the leaders trading places on margin. DraftKings led handle share at 37.6% (37.3% a year ago) and GGR share at 35.4% (34.9%) with a 9.5% gross gaming margin; FanDuel's handle share rose to 32.8% (31.4%) but GGR share fell to 35.4% (37.7%) despite the higher margin in the market at 10.4%. Fanatics ceded handle share (9.9% vs 11.2%) while lifting GGR share to 8.8% from 7.3% – evidence of a deliberate pivot from promo-driven volume to margin. Caesars' margin slipped to 6.9% from 7.6% with share losses on both metrics; BetMGM lifted margin to 10.2% from 9.6% as GGR share rose on lower handle; bet365 held 9.4%. Market-wide gross margin was flat at 9.6%, so August's hold collapse was outcome-driven rather than pricing-driven.

Commercially, the US sportsbook model in 2026 is a high-tax, high-CAC, margin-dependent business where the structural hold target (~10–11% for the leaders, via parlay/SGP mix) is being tested by both outcomes and an untaxed substitute. State treasuries are already feeling it: August sports-betting tax fell 14.0%. For a new entrant the arithmetic is unattractive – a 20–51% GGR tax in the large states, 0.25% federal excise on handle, market-access fees to a land-based partner and two incumbents with ~70% share – unless the entry thesis is B2B (pricing, trading, platform) or a differentiated niche (fixed-odds racing was just added in Michigan on 30 Oct 2026).

Watch for the AGA Q3 quarterly report in mid-November to confirm September: our estimate is that national Q3-26 SB GGR finishes roughly flat to modestly down YoY (July's +27% offset by August's -15.6% and a likely double-digit September decline on low hold), with handle up low-double-digits only because of the World Cup – i.e. underlying ex-event handle still negative.

segments.name: iGaming (online casino)
segments.headline: Still the best-growth vertical but decelerating to +12% as the seven-state footprint matures; FanDuel losing share, DraftKings and challengers gaining.
narrative: iGaming remains the only US vertical compounding at double digits, but every data point in Q3 shows deceleration. AGA monthly revenue was $1.01bn in July (+15.7%) and $1.03bn in August (+12.3%), versus +27.6% for FY2025 ($10.73bn) and +32–33% monthly growth in spring 2025. Citizens' full-quarter read is +12% YoY, the weakest on record and down from +16% in both Q1 and Q2-26. The AGA's own commentary is that with no new markets coming online the vertical is showing natural maturation. Secondary trackers put September at ~$1.02bn (unverified), which would imply Q3-26 iGaming GGR of roughly $3.05–3.10bn (estimate) versus ~$3.03bn in Q2-26 (secondary) – sequentially flat, which is itself new.

State regulators corroborate. New Jersey internet gaming win was $274.8m in September (+13.0%), $2.40bn YTD (+13.2%), and now represents 47% of total state gaming revenue versus 39% for Atlantic City floor win – the clearest demonstration anywhere of online overtaking land-based. Michigan's September iGaming gross receipts were $300.2m ($288.15m adjusted gross receipts, -0.9% MoM), with 15 authorised commercial and tribal operators. Pennsylvania remains the largest state by iGaming revenue; a secondary headline citing $555m for September could not be reconciled with prior run-rates and likely refers to total PGCB revenue – treat as unverified.

The competitive map is shifting beneath a stable top-3. Citizens has FanDuel at 25.1% (26.6% a year ago, down every quarter of 2026), DraftKings at 22.2% (24.3%, but up from 20.9% in Q2 – its first sequential gain in two years), and BetMGM at 18.6% (20.7%, sixth straight quarterly decline). Rush Street rose to 7.4% (6.8%), Caesars fell to 6.4% (7.1%), Fanatics grew fastest to 5.2% (3.9%; 5.4% in Q2) and bet365 jumped to 1.7% from 0.4% on its Michigan and West Virginia launches. Aggregate top-3 share fell from 71.6% to 65.9% in a year, which is the opening for a well-capitalised challenger with a differentiated content/CRM stack – though the share is being won by operators who already own a sportsbook funnel.

Economics remain the best in US gaming for scaled operators: state tax on iGaming GGR ranges from ~15% to 54% (PA slots) [statutory, not re-verified], but hold is structural rather than outcome-driven, product differentiation (exclusive content, live dealer studios, jackpots) is durable, and cross-sell from sportsbook lowers blended CAC. The constraint is footprint: seven live states covering roughly 15% of the US population, with Maine (tribal exclusive) the only addition on the statute book and no large state (NY, IL, MD, IN, OH) having legislated in 2025–26. Tax ratchets (NJ to 19.75% in 2025) and the federal 90% loss-deduction cap on players from TY2026 [unverified this cycle] are the policy headwinds.

For B2Tech, iGaming is the only US vertical where a B2C or B2B entry can show a path to returns: supplying platform/aggregation or live content to the 15 Michigan, ~30 New Jersey and ~20 Pennsylvania licensees [counts from prior research, unverified] is lower risk than a B2C skin, which would require a land-based partner, state-level licensing of key personnel and a marketing budget to dislodge incumbents now spending to defend share as growth slows.

segments.name: Land-based casino & retail
segments.headline: Low-single-digit growth ballast; tables outpacing slots, with New York downstate expansion the main new supply.
narrative: Traditional casino slots and tables remain two-thirds of US commercial GGR and are growing in line with nominal consumer spending: $4.48bn in July (+3.1%) and $4.44bn in August (+0.9%). Slots were flat-to-up ($3.25bn both months, +0.9% and +1.0%) while table games grew faster ($876.8m, +6.2% in July; $885.9m, +2.1% in August), with the AGA crediting Resorts World New York City's recent expansion for part of the August table gain. Figures exclude Louisiana and Michigan, which report combined slot/table revenue. FY2025 traditional casino revenue was ~$51.0bn (derived from AGA totals), implying ~2–3% underlying growth.

Regional prints were mixed in September. Atlantic City's nine casinos' floor win fell 1.3% to $227.8m even as New Jersey's total gaming revenue rose 2.8%, and the state's YTD total gaming revenue is $5.39bn (+5.1%), with gross revenue taxes of $82.7m for the month and $756.8m YTD. Detroit's three commercial casinos reported $103.55m of aggregate adjusted revenue for September (MGCB). Retail sportsbooks are a small and shrinking component; the AGA's monthly headline bundles retail SB into the sports-betting line.

The land-based tax base is the political anchor of US gaming: it funds the state programmes (pensions, education, problem-gambling) that the AGA invokes in its campaign against untaxed channels, and it is the gatekeeper for online access in most states via the skin/partner model. For an online-first entrant, land-based relevance is therefore as a licensing counterparty, not a revenue pool.

New supply to watch is concentrated in New York's three downstate casino licences (Resorts World NYC expansion already visible in the data; Bronx and Queens projects to follow) [status of other two projects unverified this cycle], continued expansion in Illinois, Virginia and Nebraska that drove 2025 growth, and Las Vegas Strip softness noted in Q3 operator results (Boyd Gaming missed estimates on weaker tourism – secondary).

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime
segments.headline: Fifty rulebooks, one direction: access via land-based partners, GGR-based taxes that only move up, and a federal layer (excise, loss-deduction cap, CFTC) that is now the live battleground.
narrative: There is no federal gambling licence. Since Murphy v. NCAA (2018) struck down PASPA, each state legislates and licenses sports betting; iGaming has always been state-level (NJ 2013 onwards); tribal gaming runs under IGRA compacts; and the federal Wire Act and UIGEA police interstate and payment flows. As of end-2025 the AGA counts 38 commercial gaming jurisdictions, 35 states with commercial sports betting (39 states plus DC and Puerto Rico including tribal-only markets such as Washington and Florida), and seven live iGaming states (NJ, PA, MI, WV, CT, DE, RI) with Nevada poker-only and Maine enacted but not launched. The dominant access model is the 'skin': an online operator must contract with a licensed casino, racetrack or tribe, except in a minority of open-market states (e.g. Tennessee, Wyoming, DC).

Licensing cost and friction scale with state size. Statutory headline fees range from ~$100k in New Jersey to $25m in New York (mobile), $20m for an Illinois online-only licence, $10m-class fees in Pennsylvania for each of sportsbook and iGaming, $5m in Massachusetts and low-single-digit millions elsewhere [all from prior research; not re-verified this cycle]. Beyond fees, every state requires suitability investigation of the entity and key persons, independent lab certification of platform and games, in-state geolocation and KYC, and usually in-state or US-based servers; licence terms are typically 3–5 years with renewal fees. Michigan's 15 licensees (13 OSB, 15 iGaming) illustrate the capped-skin structure – one per land-based or tribal licensee.

Tax is levied on GGR (gross win, in several states net of promotional deductions that are being phased down) at the state level, plus a federal excise of 0.25% of sports handle and $50 per employee. Headline online sports-betting rates run from 6.75% (Nevada) through 10–15% (Missouri, Virginia, Colorado, Kentucky-class), 18–21.5% (North Carolina, Ohio, Massachusetts, Maryland, Louisiana), 19.75% (New Jersey), 20–40% tiered plus $0.25–0.50 per wager (Illinois), 36% (Pennsylvania) to 51% (New York, Rhode Island). iGaming rates range from ~15% to 54% on PA slots. 2025 was a ratchet year – NJ (13%/15% to 19.75%), Maryland (15% to 20%), Louisiana (15% to 21.5%), Illinois' per-wager surcharge which prompted FanDuel/DraftKings to add a $0.50 customer fee – and the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act capped the player gambling-loss deduction at 90% of losses from tax year 2026 [all background; unverified this cycle]. No comparable state rate change was identified for Q3-26, but the AGA's tax-take data (August -1.5%, SB tax -14.0%) will add pressure in 2027 sessions.

Tax take is large and visible: $17.86bn in FY2025 (+12.3%), $1.42bn in July 2026 (+7.7%) and $1.46bn in August (-1.5%). The AGA's framing – that prediction markets, sweepstakes casinos and skill machines pay no state gaming tax and have cost states an estimated $1.56bn since January 2025 – has been adopted by regulators, 16 of which had taken enforcement action against event-contract platforms by May 2026. This matters for the rulebook because it realigns the licensed industry and state treasuries against a federally-regulated channel (CFTC-designated contract markets), with the courts deciding whether the Commodity Exchange Act pre-empts state gaming law.

For an operator the practical implications are: (i) effective tax burden in the large states (NY 51%, PA 36%, IL up to 40% + per-bet) makes sportsbook profitability a scale game; (ii) iGaming taxes are high but offset by structural hold; (iii) every state is a separate licence, lab certification and reporting regime, so compliance headcount scales with footprint; (iv) the direction of travel is up on tax, tighter on promo deductibility and more restrictive on advertising, with the only liberalising moves being product (fixed-odds racing in Michigan) and the slow spread of iGaming.

segments.name: Prediction markets, sweepstakes & enforcement
segments.headline: The defining regulatory fight of 2026: CFTC-regulated sports event contracts are pulling handle and tax out of the state system; states are suing, fining and, in Michigan's case, winning climbdowns.
narrative: The AGA's monthly trackers have, since mid-2026, carried a standing paragraph attributing lost state tax to three untaxed channels: skill machines, sweepstakes casinos and sports betting offered through prediction-market platforms. The cumulative estimate of foregone gaming tax from event contracts rose from ~$1.5bn (July tracker) to over $1.56bn (August tracker) since January 2025 – an advocacy estimate of potential tax on displaced handle, not an assessed liability, but one that is now driving legislative and enforcement behaviour. The August data gave it teeth: handle -0.7%, SB tax -14.0%, and an explicit statement that ex-World Cup handle has been negative YoY since December 2025.

The legal structure of the conflict is federal pre-emption. Platforms such as Kalshi, Crypto.com and Polymarket US offer sports-outcome contracts as CFTC-designated contract markets in all 50 states, arguing the Commodity Exchange Act exclusively governs them; states respond that the contracts are sports wagers under state law. By May 2026 the AGA counted 16 states with enforcement action (cease-and-desist letters, litigation) [background on specific 2025 cases – Nevada, New Jersey, Maryland, Massachusetts, Ohio, Illinois, Michigan – from prior research, not re-verified]. The Q3-26 marker is Michigan: on 28 Oct 2026 the MGCB announced that QCX LLC (Polymarket US) agreed to stop offering new sports-related contracts in the state, which the regulator framed as part of a continuing crackdown on unlicensed sports betting. Licensed operators have hedged by launching their own event-contract products (DraftKings and FanDuel both announced prediction-market ventures in late 2025 – background, unverified), so the industry's position is now 'regulate and tax, or compete'.

Sweepstakes casinos are the second front. A wave of 2025 state bans (including Montana, Connecticut, Nevada, New Jersey, New York and California – background) pushed the largest operators to exit those states, and the AGA continues to cite them as a tax leak; expect further bans and attorney-general actions in 2027 sessions. Skill machines (unregulated slot-like terminals in bars and convenience stores, concentrated in Pennsylvania, Virginia and Texas) are the third, and the one most likely to be resolved by regulation-and-tax rather than prohibition.

The commercial read for an entrant is double-edged. If courts or Congress affirm state jurisdiction, the licensed channel recovers handle and the tax base; if federal pre-emption prevails, the lowest-tax route into US sports betting becomes a CFTC licence (or a partnership with a DCM) rather than 35 state licences – a structural threat to the skin/partner model and to state tax revenues that would force a federal-state settlement. Either way, the next 12 months of appellate rulings and any CFTC rulemaking are the single largest swing factor for US market structure since PASPA.

Enforcement against licensed operators continues in parallel – advertising, RG and geolocation fines are routine – but the volume and political salience of actions is now overwhelmingly directed at unlicensed channels, which is a favourable backdrop for a compliant licensee and a hostile one for grey-market entry.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling & advertising
segments.headline: Card/ACH rails with state-level credit bans; RG and advertising rules tightening incrementally and state-by-state, with promo deductibility the commercial pressure point.
narrative: US online gambling payments are bank-rail based: debit cards, ACH/e-check (VIP Preferred), PayPal/Venmo, Apple Pay, prepaid 'Play+' cards and cash-at-retailer (PayNearMe). Credit-card deposits are prohibited in a growing set of states (Massachusetts, Iowa and Tennessee among them, with New York and others debating bans) and many issuers block gambling MCC codes regardless; crypto is not an accepted deposit method on licensed sites. Withdrawals typically clear in 1–3 days via ACH or instant to debit. [All background from prior research; no Q3-26 change identified.] Promotional credits remain large relative to revenue – Michigan's September online SB adjusted gross receipts of $24.89m against $55.5m gross receipts shows promo deductions consuming more than half of gross win in the NFL kick-off month – and states are progressively capping or phasing out promo deductibility, which raises effective tax rates without changing headline rates.

Responsible-gambling architecture is state-mandated and fragmented: statewide self-exclusion registries, mandatory deposit/time/loss limit tools, age 21 in nearly all states, problem-gambling funding carved from tax receipts, and a 1-800-GAMBLER helpline mandate in advertising. Several states (e.g. New Jersey) have moved to require operators to monitor and intervene on at-risk play patterns [background]. The federal 90% loss-deduction cap from TY2026 is, perversely, the biggest player-economics change of the cycle and could push high-volume bettors toward untaxed venues.

Advertising is governed by state regulation plus the AGA Responsible Marketing Code: no targeting under-21s or college campuses, no 'risk-free' language (Ohio, Massachusetts and others), mandatory RG messaging, and a broadening set of restrictions on college-athlete player props following NCAA lobbying [background]. The macro trend is that total gaming ad volume is falling as operators cut CAC in a maturing market, which reduces political heat but also raises the bar for a new brand to achieve awareness.

For an entrant, the compliance stack – payment-processor relationships willing to onboard gambling MCCs, KYC/geolocation vendors certified per state, RG tooling and reporting, and advertising pre-clearance in stricter states – is a 6–12-month build and a recurring cost that scales linearly with the number of states. It is best shared via a B2B platform or an established market-access partner rather than built de novo for a single-state launch.

highlights.text: Largest regulated online pool globally: FY2025 SB + iGaming GGR of $27.6bn (AGA) and still growing in aggregate; iGaming alone at a ~$12bn+ annualised run-rate (Aug-26 $1.03bn x12) with structural hold.

iGaming oligopoly is loosening: top-3 share fell from 71.6% to 65.9% in a year (Citizens), with Fanatics (+1.3pp), Rush Street (+0.6pp) and bet365 (+1.3pp) proving that late entrants can take share in the seven live states.

Enforcement is now aimed at unlicensed channels (prediction markets, sweepstakes, skill machines) rather than licensees; Michigan's Polymarket climbdown (28 Oct 2026) and 16 states' actions create a favourable backdrop for compliant operators and B2B suppliers.

Product liberalisation continues at the margin – fixed-odds horse racing added to Michigan online sportsbooks (30 Oct 2026); New York downstate casino expansion (Resorts World NYC) is adding land-based supply and future online skins.

State revenue dependence creates a lobby for new iGaming legislation: SB tax fell 14% in August and NJ iGaming now generates 47% of state gaming revenue, which strengthens the fiscal case for NY/IL/MD-class states to legalise online casino in 2027 sessions.

World Cup proved event-driven upside: July handle +31.9% and SB GGR +27.0% show latent demand that reactivates with major events (2028 Olympics/Euro-free summer aside), useful for promotional planning.

lowlights.text: Sports-betting GGR is contracting: August -15.6% YoY to $1.00bn on 9.2% hold, NJ SB GGR -6.3% YTD, and the AGA says ex-World Cup handle has fallen YoY every month since December 2025 – the first structural volume decline since PASPA.

Untaxed federal-licensed substitute: CFTC-regulated sports event contracts are pulling handle (AGA est. $1.56bn tax foregone since Jan-25) and the pre-emption question is unresolved in the courts – a binary risk to the state skin/tax model.
iGaming growth has halved: +12% in Q3-26 (Citizens) vs +27.6% in FY25 and +32–33% in spring 2025, with no new state launch since 2024 and Maine (small, tribal) the only enacted addition.

Tax ratchet with no ceiling: 2025 hikes in NJ (19.75%), MD (20%), LA (21.5%) and IL (20–40% + per-wager) plus the federal 90% loss-deduction cap from TY2026; shrinking SB tax receipts in 2026 make further 2027 increases more, not less, likely.

Entry economics for B2C sportsbook are prohibitive: DraftKings + FanDuel hold 70.8% of GGR, market access requires a land-based partner and $100k–$25m per-state fees, and Michigan data show promos still absorbing >50% of gross win in NFL months.

Data gap on the quarter: AGA's Q3-26 quarterly report (incl. September) was not yet published and web-tool budget was exhausted mid-research; September national figures and several statutory rates in this brief are secondary or unverified and must be confirmed before use.

forecast.intro: The bridge from FY2025's record $78.62bn (+9.1%) to the 2026 run-rate is driven almost entirely by sports betting: July's World Cup spike (+27.0% SB GGR) gave way to an August collapse (-15.6%) on hold normalisation (9.2%) and flat handle, while iGaming decelerated from +27.6% (FY25) to +12% (Q3-26, Citizens) and land-based held at +1–3%. Jul+Aug-26 total commercial GGR is $13.24bn, +3.9% YoY (computed from AGA monthly data). The moving parts for the rest of 2026 are September–December sportsbook hold (NY September reportedly 6.6%), the pace of prediction-market leakage, and whether any state changes tax or product rules before year-end (none identified for Q3).

bridge.title: Jul-26: World Cup lifts SB GGR

forecast.view: **Our independent view (all figures estimates):** FY2026 US commercial GGR grows **~+2–4%** to roughly **$80–82bn**, the slowest since the 2020 reopening, with **iGaming +13–15% (~$12.2–12.4bn)**, **traditional casino +1–2%**, and **sports-betting GGR flat to -5%** as hold normalises to ~9.5–10% and prediction markets absorb a mid-single-digit share of handle. Q3-26 national SB GGR likely finishes **flat to modestly down YoY** (July +27% offset by August -15.6% and a weak September); Q3 iGaming ~**$3.05–3.10bn (+12–14%)**. State tax take should still rise ~2–4% for the year on iGaming mix but SB tax will decline. **Regulatory direction over 12–24 months:** (1) tax rates move only upward – expect at least two more states to raise online SB rates or cut promo deductibility in 2027 sessions; (2) event contracts are the swing factor – a pro-state appellate ruling or CFTC rulemaking requiring state deference would restore handle to licensees, a pro-pre-emption outcome would force a federal-state settlement and compress the value of state skins; (3) iGaming expansion resumes slowly – Maine launches, one additional mid-size state (we would weight NY/IL/MD as possible but not probable before 2028); (4) sweepstakes prohibitions spread to a majority of states; (5) advertising and college-prop restrictions tighten incrementally. **For B2Tech:** prioritise B2B supply (platform, content, pricing) into the seven iGaming states and any new launch state; treat B2C sportsbook entry as uneconomic absent a distinctive product or a federal event-contract route; monitor the pre-emption litigation as the gating item for any US capital commitment.
watch: AGA Q3-26 quarterly Commercial Gaming Revenue Tracker (expected mid-Nov 2026) – confirms September and full-quarter SB/iGaming prints; verify our Q3 estimates.
Appellate rulings and any CFTC rulemaking on sports event contracts (Kalshi/Polymarket/Crypto.com vs states) – the pre-emption outcome is the single largest structural swing factor.

September–November state prints: NY mobile hold (6.6% reported for Sept, unverified), NJ SB GGR trajectory (-6.3% YTD), Michigan promo-deduction burden, and whether ex-event handle turns positive with the NFL season.
2027 state legislative calendar: tax-rate bills, promo-deductibility caps, iGaming bills in NY/IL/MD/IN, sweepstakes bans, college-prop restrictions; Maine iGaming launch timing.
Federal: implementation of the 90% gambling-loss deduction cap (TY2026) and any FAIR BET Act repeal effort; SAFE Bet Act / GRIT Act federal-standards proposals.
Operator behaviour: FanDuel iGaming share erosion, DraftKings' sequential rebound, Fanatics/bet365 share gains, and licensed operators' own event-contract launches as a hedge.
